name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Biological definition of plant growth

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements best defines plant growth in biological terms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understanding the concept of growth
Growth is one of the most fundamental and conspicuous characteristics of living beings. In plants and other organisms, it is characterized by an irreversible, permanent increase in the size of an organ, an organ part, or an individual cell.

Step 2: Energy requirement and metabolic coupling
True growth is accompanied by both anabolic and catabolic metabolic processes that proceed at the expense of metabolic energy. Reversible physical phenomena, such as the swelling of dry wood placed in water (imbibition), do not constitute biological growth because they are not irreversible and do not involve metabolic energy expenditure.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, growth is strictly an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ or its parts or an individual cell, accompanied by metabolic processes at the expense of energy.

answer.text: An irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts, or an individual cell, accompanied by metabolic processes
A reversible swelling of cellular structures caused purely by passive physical water imbibition
A temporary increase in fresh weight occurring independently of metabolic energy and enzymatic action
An increase in protoplasmic mass without any corresponding change in cell volume, length, or cell number

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Open form of growth in plants

questiontext.text: Plant growth is described as an "open form of growth" primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the role of meristems
Plants retain the capacity for unlimited and indeterminate growth throughout their lifetime due to the persistence of localized meristematic tissues at specific sites in their body.

Step 2: Defining open growth
The cells of these meristems have the capacity to continuously divide and self-perpetuate. As a result, new cells are continuously added to the plant body by the activity of these meristems. This mode of development, where new cells are constantly added, is termed the open form of growth.

Step 3: Conclusion
The open form of growth signifies that new cells are continuously being added to the plant body by the perpetual dividing activity of meristematic cells.

answer.text: New cells are continuously added to the plant body by the ongoing activity of meristems
All organs grow without any fixed shape and continue to expand indefinitely throughout the life cycle
Growth occurs without any regulation by internal genetic factors or plant hormones
Differentiated cells never lose their ability to divide regardless of location

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Meristems responsible for secondary growth

questiontext.text: In gymnosperms and dicotyledonous plants, an increase in the girth of organs is caused by lateral meristems. Which lateral meristems are responsible for this secondary growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Distinguishing primary and secondary growth
Root apical meristems and shoot apical meristems contribute to primary growth, which principally accounts for elongation along the plant axis.

Step 2: Identifying lateral meristems
In dicotyledons and gymnosperms, lateral meristems appear later in life. These lateral meristems comprise vascular cambium and cork-cambium (phellogen), which divide periclinally to increase the diameter or girth of stems and roots, constituting secondary growth.

Step 3: Conclusion
The specific lateral meristems responsible for secondary growth are the vascular cambium and cork-cambium.

answer.text: Vascular cambium and cork-cambium
Root apical meristem and shoot apical meristem
Intercalary meristem and apical meristem
Dermatogen and procambium exclusively

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Parameters used to measure cellular growth

questiontext.text: At the cellular level, growth is principally a consequence of an increase in the amount of protoplasm. Because this is difficult to measure directly, various parameters proportional to it are utilized. Which of the following correctly pairs a biological structure with the parameter generally used to express its growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reviewing parameters of growth from NCERT
- Growth of a pollen tube is measured in terms of its length.
- Growth in a dorsiventral leaf is measured by an increase in surface area.
- Growth in a single maize root apical meristem is expressed as an increase in cell number (over 17,500 new cells per hour).
- Growth in cells of watermelon is expressed as an increase in the size/volume of the cell (up to 350,000 times).

Step 2: Evaluating the correct pairing
Matching pollen tube with length, dorsiventral leaf with surface area, and maize apical meristem with cell number shows that measuring pollen tube growth in terms of length is an accurate correlation.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct match is pollen tube growth measured in terms of length.

answer.text: Pollen tube — Length
Dorsiventral leaf — Cell number exclusively
Watermelon fruit cells — Increase in cell number per hour
Maize root apical meristem — Increase in cell size up to 350,000 times

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Rate of cell addition by maize root apical meristem

questiontext.text: A single apical meristem of a maize root can give rise to more than how many new cells per hour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Direct fact retrieval from textbook
According to NCERT Chapter 13 (Section 13.1.2), growth expressed as an increase in cell number is demonstrated by the maize root apical meristem.

Step 2: Quantitative value
A single maize root apical meristem can produce more than 17,500 new cells per hour.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct quantitative benchmark is 17,500 new cells per hour.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Cellular characteristics of the meristematic zone

questiontext.text: Which set of cellular characteristics is distinctive of the cells in the meristematic phase of growth at root and shoot apices?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying features of the meristematic phase
The cells in the meristematic phase (at root and shoot apex) divide constantly. They are rich in protoplasm and possess large, conspicuous nuclei.

Step 2: Cell wall characteristics
Their cell walls are primary in nature, thin, cellulosic, and have abundant plasmodesmatal connections.

Step 3: Contrast with other phases
Increased vacuolation and enlargement characterize the elongation phase, while heavy lignified wall thickenings characterize the maturation phase.

Step 4: Conclusion
The correct combination of features is: rich in protoplasm, large conspicuous nuclei, thin cellulosic primary walls, and abundant plasmodesmatal connections.

answer.text: Rich in protoplasm, large conspicuous nuclei, thin cellulosic primary cell walls, and abundant plasmodesmata
High degree of vacuolation, thick lignified secondary walls, and absence of plasmodesmata
Maximal cell size, degenerate nuclei, and highly thickened suberized walls
Devoid of conspicuous nuclei, dense secondary cell wall deposition, and low enzymatic activity

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristics of the phase of elongation

questiontext.text: Cells proximal to the meristematic zone represent the phase of elongation. What are the key cellular features associated with this phase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Locating the zone of elongation
The cells positioned proximal (immediately adjacent, further away from the apex) to the meristematic zone enter the phase of elongation.

Step 2: Identifying cellular modifications
The NCERT text highlights three prominent features of the elongation phase: increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition.

Step 3: Conclusion
The hallmarks of the elongation phase are increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and deposition of new cell wall material.

answer.text: Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition
Lignification of secondary walls and total loss of cellular protoplasm
Continuous mitotic cell divisions and formation of large conspicuous nuclei
Loss of turgor and shrinkage of central vacuolar compartments

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Characteristics of the phase of maturation

questiontext.text: The portion of the plant axis lying further away from the apex, proximal to the phase of elongation, undergoes the phase of maturation. Cells in this zone are distinguished by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Locating the maturation zone
Lying proximal to the elongation zone, cells in the maturation zone reach their terminal structural specializations.

Step 2: Cellular modifications in maturation
Cells attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications, leading to differentiation into specialized cell types and tissues (such as tracheary elements, fibers, and parenchyma).

Step 3: Conclusion
Attaining maximal size regarding wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications defines the phase of maturation.

answer.text: Attaining maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications
Rapid rate of mitotic cell divisions with thin primary cellulosic walls
Initial development of vacuoles with high rates of longitudinal expansion
Loss of cell wall and reversion to naked protoplasts

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Cell division fate in arithmetic growth

questiontext.text: In arithmetic growth, following mitotic cell division, what is the fate of the resulting daughter cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of arithmetic growth
In arithmetic growth, cell division yields two daughter cells with unequal developmental fates.

Step 2: Progeny behavior
Only one daughter cell continues to divide, whereas the other daughter cell differentiates and matures, ceasing division.

Step 3: Contrast with geometric growth
In geometric growth, both daughter cells retain the ability to divide and continue mitotic division.

Step 4: Conclusion
In arithmetic growth, only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures.

answer.text: Only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures
Both daughter cells retain the capacity to divide perpetually
Both daughter cells undergo immediate senescence and death
One daughter cell dies while the other divides by meiosis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Mathematical expression of arithmetic growth

questiontext.text: The mathematical expression for arithmetic growth is \(L_t = L_0 + rt\). What does the parameter \(r\) represent in this equation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula definition
The equation \(L_t = L_0 + rt\) describes linear arithmetic growth, exemplified by a root elongating at a constant rate.

Step 2: Component breakdown
- \(L_t\) = length at time \(t\)
- \(L_0\) = initial length at time zero
- \(r\) = growth rate or elongation per unit time
- \(t\) = time

Step 3: Conclusion
The parameter \(r\) denotes the growth rate or elongation per unit time.

answer.text: Growth rate or elongation per unit time
Base of natural logarithms
Relative efficiency index of nutrient uptake
Total duration of the lag phase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q11 - Sigmoid curve stages in natural growth

questiontext.text: When the growth parameter of a plant organ growing in a natural environment is plotted against time, a typical S-shaped (sigmoid) curve is obtained. What is the correct sequence of phases observed in this curve?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyzing the sigmoid growth curve
In living organisms growing in a natural environment with initially unlimiting and subsequently limiting resources, growth is typically geometric initially before slowing down.

Step 2: Identifying the phases in temporal order
1. Initial phase is slow: Lag phase.
2. Growth increases rapidly at an exponential rate: Log phase (or exponential phase).
3. Nutrient supply becomes limiting, and growth slows down: Stationary phase.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct developmental sequence is: Lag phase → Log (exponential) phase → Stationary phase.

answer.text: Lag phase → Log (exponential) phase → Stationary phase
Log phase → Lag phase → Stationary phase
Stationary phase → Exponential phase → Lag phase
Lag phase → Stationary phase → Log phase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q12 - Efficiency index in exponential growth equation

questiontext.text: In the exponential growth equation \(W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}\), what does the term \(r\) represent with respect to plant performance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula definition
In \(W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}\):
- \(W_1\) = final size (weight, height, number)
- \(W_0\) = initial size at the beginning of the period
- \(t\) = time of growth
- \(e\) = base of natural logarithms

Step 2: Interpretation of \(r\)
Here, \(r\) is the relative growth rate and is also a measure of the ability of the plant to produce new plant material, which is referred to as the efficiency index.

Step 3: Conclusion
\(r\) represents the relative growth rate and efficiency index of the plant.

answer.text: Relative growth rate and the efficiency index of the plant to produce new material
Absolute growth rate independent of initial biomass
Total final weight attained after senescence
Base of natural logarithms equal to approximately 2.718

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q13 - Comparison of absolute and relative growth rates of leaves

questiontext.text: Leaf A has an initial surface area of \(5\text{ cm}^2\) and expands to \(10\text{ cm}^2\) in a given time period. Leaf B has an initial surface area of \(50\text{ cm}^2\) and expands to \(55\text{ cm}^2\) over the same time period. Which of the following statements correctly compares their growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate Absolute Growth Rate (AGR)
AGR is total growth per unit time.
For Leaf A: \(\Delta \text{Area} = 10\text{ cm}^2 - 5\text{ cm}^2 = 5\text{ cm}^2\).
For Leaf B: \(\Delta \text{Area} = 55\text{ cm}^2 - 50\text{ cm}^2 = 5\text{ cm}^2\).
Thus, both leaves have an identical absolute growth rate (\(5\text{ cm}^2\) per given time).

Step 2: Calculate Relative Growth Rate (RGR)
RGR is growth per unit time expressed per unit initial parameter.
For Leaf A: \(\text{RGR} = \frac{5}{5} \times 100\% = 100\%\).
For Leaf B: \(\text{RGR} = \frac{5}{50} \times 100\% = 10\%\).

Step 3: Conclusion
Both leaves have the same absolute growth rate, but Leaf A has a much higher relative growth rate.

answer.text: Both leaves exhibit the same absolute growth rate, but Leaf A exhibits a higher relative growth rate
Leaf B exhibits a higher absolute growth rate and a higher relative growth rate
Both leaves exhibit identical absolute and relative growth rates
Leaf A exhibits a higher absolute growth rate, but Leaf B exhibits a higher relative growth rate

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q14 - Role of water and turgidity in cell enlargement

questiontext.text: How does water primarily facilitate extension growth during the cell enlargement phase in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of water in cell enlargement
Plant cells enlarge predominantly by taking up water into the vacuole. Turgidity generated by this uptake provides the necessary mechanical hydrostatic pressure that stretches the cell wall, driving extension growth.

Step 2: Additional physiological roles of water
Water also provides the aqueous medium for various enzymatic activities essential for growth metabolism.

Step 3: Conclusion
Cell enlargement depends intimately on cell turgidity driving wall extension, alongside providing the enzymatic medium.

answer.text: Turgidity of cells provides mechanical hydrostatic pressure that helps in extension growth
Water acts as a competitive inhibitor of lytic enzymes in the primary cell wall
Water hydrolyzes pectin microfibrils into glucose without cellular turgor
Water directly provides metabolic ATP required for microtubule assembly

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q15 - Differentiation process in tracheary element formation

questiontext.text: During the differentiation of a meristematic cell into a functional tracheary element, which of the following major structural modifications occurs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understanding differentiation
Differentiation involves structural and functional specializations that cells undergo upon maturing.

Step 2: Modifications in tracheary elements
To conduct water efficiently under high negative tension over long distances, cells destined to become tracheary elements lose their protoplasm completely. In addition, they develop strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls to withstand collapse.

Step 3: Conclusion
Formation of a tracheary element involves the loss of protoplasm and the development of strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls.

answer.text: Loss of protoplasm and deposition of strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls
Expansion of the nucleus and retention of thin primary cellulosic walls
Deposition of suberin along with maintenance of active cytoplasm
Conversion of cellulose to pectin without change in protoplasmic content

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q16 - Examples of dedifferentiation in plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following tissues is an example of a product formed through the phenomenon of dedifferentiation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of dedifferentiation
Dedifferentiation is the phenomenon where living differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide regain the capacity to divide under certain conditions.

Step 2: Identifying textbook examples
NCERT explicitly identifies the formation of meristems—specifically interfascicular cambium and cork cambium (phellogen)—from fully differentiated cortical or parenchymal cells as dedifferentiation.

Step 3: Evaluating secondary products
Secondary xylem, cork (phellem), and secondary cortex (phelloderm) are the products of redifferentiation.

Step 4: Conclusion
Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium are formed by dedifferentiation.

answer.text: Interfascicular cambium
Tracheary elements
Cork (phellem)
Root cap cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q17 - Identifying products of redifferentiation

questiontext.text: Which of the following structures in a woody dicotyledonous stem is a product of redifferentiation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understanding redifferentiation
Dedifferentiated meristematic cells (such as interfascicular cambium or cork cambium) divide and produce cells that once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions. This process is redifferentiation.

Step 2: Identifying tissues formed
Tissues produced by the activity of cork cambium (such as cork and secondary cortex) and vascular cambium (such as secondary xylem and secondary phloem) are products of redifferentiation.

Step 3: Conclusion
Cork tissue is formed through redifferentiation.

answer.text: Cork tissue
Cork cambium
Interfascicular cambium
Shoot apical meristem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q18 - Position-dependent open differentiation in root tips

questiontext.text: Differentiation in plants is described as "open" because cells arising from the same meristem develop into different structures depending on their location. What do cells derived from the root apical meristem differentiate into when pushed towards the periphery?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of open differentiation
The final structure at maturity of a cell or tissue is determined by the location of the cell within the plant body.

Step 2: Examples given in NCERT
- Cells positioned away from root apical meristem (distal/outermost root tip direction) differentiate as root-cap cells.
- Cells pushed towards the periphery mature as epidermis (epiblema).

Step 3: Conclusion
Cells pushed to the periphery differentiate into the epidermis.

answer.text: Epidermis
Root-cap cells
Endodermis
Vascular bundle xylem vessels

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q19 - Sequence of developmental processes in a plant cell

questiontext.text: According to the schematic representation of the developmental process of a plant cell, what is the correct sequence of events from a meristematic cell to death?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyzing the developmental sequence
According to NCERT Figure 13.8, a meristematic cell undergoes:
1. Plasmatic growth
2. Cell division / Expansion (Elongation)
3. Differentiation
4. Maturation leading to a mature cell
5. Senescence
6. Death

Step 2: Verifying the sequential progression
Meristematic cell → Plasmatic growth → Expansion (elongation) → Maturation → Mature cell → Senescence → Death.

Step 3: Conclusion
The sequence begins with plasmatic growth, proceeds through cell expansion, differentiation/maturation into a mature cell, followed by senescence and death.

answer.text: Plasmatic growth → Cell expansion → Maturation → Mature cell → Senescence → Death
Maturation → Cell expansion → Plasmatic growth → Senescence → Death
Senescence → Maturation → Cell expansion → Mature cell → Death
Cell expansion → Senescence → Plasmatic growth → Maturation → Death

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q20 - Plasticity manifested as environmental heterophylly

questiontext.text: Plants follow different pathways in response to environment or phases of life to form different structures; this ability is called plasticity. Which of the following is an example of heterophylly induced by environmental variation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Differentiating types of heterophylly
Plasticity is shown as heterophylly in two major contexts:
1. Heterophylly due to phases of life (juvenile vs adult): cotton, coriander, and larkspur.
2. Heterophylly due to habitat/environment (terrestrial vs aquatic habitat): buttercup.

Step 2: Analyzing buttercup
In buttercup, leaves produced in air are broad and lobed, while leaves produced submerged in water are highly dissected and filamentous. This represents plasticity in response to environment.

Step 3: Conclusion
Buttercup demonstrates heterophylly triggered by environmental differences.

answer.text: Difference in shapes between terrestrial and submerged leaves in buttercup
Difference in leaf shape between juvenile and mature plants in cotton
Difference in leaf shape between juvenile and adult stages in coriander
Difference in leaf shape between juvenile and adult stages in larkspur

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q21 - Life-phase dependent heterophylly plants

questiontext.text: In which of the following groups of plants is heterophylly an expression of plasticity during different phases of life (juvenile vs mature)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying developmental heterophylly
In certain plants, the leaves of juvenile plants differ distinctively in shape from those in mature plants.

Step 2: Examples from the text
NCERT explicitly states: "heterophylly in cotton, coriander and larkspur. In such plants, the leaves of the juvenile plant are different in shape from those in mature plants."

Step 3: Conclusion
Cotton, coriander, and larkspur exhibit developmental heterophylly across phases of life.

answer.text: Cotton, coriander, and larkspur
Buttercup, sunflower, and maize
Pea, wheat, and sugarcane
Rice, tobacco, and pineapple

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q22 - Chemical nature of kinetin plant growth regulator

questiontext.text: Chemically, the cytokinin "kinetin" is classified as which of the following compounds?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying chemical classifications of PGRs
NCERT provides the chemical nature of key PGRs:
- Indole compounds: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA)
- Adenine derivatives: \(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine (kinetin)
- Carotenoid derivatives: Abscisic acid (ABA)
- Terpenes: Gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\))
- Gases: Ethylene (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\))

Step 2: Conclusion
Kinetin is an adenine derivative (\(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine).

answer.text: Adenine derivative (\(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine)
Indole compound
Carotenoid derivative
Terpene derivative

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q23 - Chemical nature of abscisic acid and gibberellic acid

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs abscisic acid (ABA) and gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\)) with their chemical nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the chemical nature of ABA and GA3
- Abscisic acid (ABA) is a derivative of carotenoids.
- Gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\)) belongs chemically to terpenes.

Step 2: Conclusion
ABA is a derivative of carotenoids, and gibberellic acid is a terpene.

answer.text: ABA is a derivative of carotenoids; \(\text{GA}_3\) is a terpene
ABA is an adenine derivative; \(\text{GA}_3\) is an indole compound
ABA is a terpene; \(\text{GA}_3\) is a carotenoid derivative
ABA is a gaseous derivative; \(\text{GA}_3\) is a purine derivative

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q24 - Functional classification of plant growth regulators

questiontext.text: Plant growth regulators (PGRs) are broadly classified into growth promoters and growth inhibitors. Which phytohormone can fit either group functionally, but is largely an inhibitor of growth activities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying functional groups
- Plant growth promoters: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins (involved in cell division, cell enlargement, flowering, fruiting).
- Plant growth inhibitors: Abscisic acid (involved in dormancy, abscission, stress responses).

Step 2: Dual status of ethylene
NCERT explicitly notes: "The gaseous PGR, ethylene, could fit either of the groups, but it is largely an inhibitor of growth activities."

Step 3: Conclusion
Ethylene fits both groups but functions largely as an inhibitor.

answer.text: Ethylene
Auxin
Gibberellin
Cytokinin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q25 - Darwin experiment on phototropism site

questiontext.text: In their classic phototropism experiments on canary grass (Phalaris canariensis), Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin concluded that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical context of Darwin experiments
Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin observed that canary grass coleoptiles bent toward unilateral light.

Step 2: Experimental deduction
By shielding different parts of the coleoptile (e.g. opaque caps over the tip vs translucent coverings), they concluded that the tip of the coleoptile was the site of a transmittable influence that caused the bending of the entire coleoptile.

Step 3: Conclusion
The tip of the coleoptile is the site of transmittable influence responsible for phototropic curvature.

answer.text: The tip of the coleoptile is the site of a transmittable influence causing bending of the coleoptile
The base of the coleoptile perceives light and synthesizes gibberellins
Auxin is destroyed on the shaded side of the coleoptile
Ethylene gas is released by the coleoptile tip causing lateral growth

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q26 - Discovery and isolation of auxin by Went

questiontext.text: Auxin was first isolated by F.W. Went from which of the following biological sources?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying Went's discovery
F.W. Went performed experiments collecting the growth-promoting substance on agar blocks.

Step 2: Source material
He isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat (Avena sativa) seedlings.

Step 3: Conclusion
Auxin was isolated by Went from oat coleoptile tips.

answer.text: Tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings
Sterile filtrate of Gibberella fujikuroi
Autoclaved herring sperm DNA
Endosperm of corn kernels

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q27 - Discovery of gibberellins and foolish seedling disease

questiontext.text: The 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice seedlings led to the discovery of gibberellins. This disease is caused by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical etiology of bakanae disease
The disease causes excessive, spindly elongation of infected rice seedlings.

Step 2: Pathogen identification and discovery
It is caused by the fungal pathogen Gibberella fujikuroi. In 1926, E. Kurosawa reported that sterile filtrates of this fungus induced the same symptoms in healthy seedlings. The active compound was later identified as gibberellic acid.

Step 3: Conclusion
The disease is caused by the fungal pathogen Gibberella fujikuroi.

answer.text: A fungal pathogen, Gibberella fujikuroi
A bacterium, Agrobacterium tumefaciens
A plant virus causing internode elongation
A root-knot nematode, Meloidogyne incognita

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q28 - Proliferation of tobacco callus and discovery of kinetin

questiontext.text: F. Skoog and co-workers observed that callus from internodal segments of tobacco stems proliferated only if the auxin-containing nutrient medium was supplemented with which of the following?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying Skoog's observations
Skoog and his colleagues investigated factors triggering cellular proliferation in tobacco pith/internodal segments.

Step 2: Required supplements
Callus proliferated only if auxins were supplemented with one of the following: extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA.

Step 3: Subsequent isolation
Miller et al. (1955) later crystallized kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA.

Step 4: Conclusion
The effective supplements included extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA.

answer.text: Extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA
Sterile filtrates of Gibberella fujikuroi
Human urine extracts rich in indole derivatives
Volatile gases collected from ripening oranges

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q29 - Chemical characterization and identity of abscisic acid

questiontext.text: During the mid-1960s, three independent research groups purified and characterized three different inhibitors: inhibitor-B, abscission II, and dormin. What was subsequently established about these substances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the inhibitors
Three distinct inhibitors were isolated independently: inhibitor-B, abscission II, and dormin.

Step 2: Discovering chemical identity
Later, chemical analysis proved that all three compounds were chemically identical. This common molecule was officially named abscisic acid (ABA).

Step 3: Conclusion
All three inhibitors proved to be chemically identical and were named abscisic acid (ABA).

answer.text: All three were chemically identical and were named abscisic acid
They were isomers of indole-3-acetic acid
They were volatile precursors of ethylene gas
They represented different oxidation states of gibberellic acid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q30 - Cousins discovery of ethylene from ripened oranges

questiontext.text: In 1910, H.H. Cousins confirmed the release of a volatile substance from ripened oranges that hastened the ripening of stored unripened bananas. What was this substance later identified as?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying Cousins' discovery
H.H. Cousins showed that volatile emanations from ripe oranges accelerated the ripening of green bananas stored nearby.

Step 2: Chemical identification
The volatile substance was subsequently confirmed to be the simple hydrocarbon gas, ethylene (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)).

Step 3: Conclusion
The volatile ripening substance was identified as ethylene.

answer.text: Ethylene
Zeatin
Abscisic acid
Gibberellic acid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q31 - Distinction between natural and synthetic auxins

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs contains only synthetic auxins widely applied in agriculture and horticulture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying natural vs synthetic auxins
- Natural auxins isolated directly from plants: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) and indole butyric acid (IBA).
- Synthetic auxins synthesized chemically: Naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) and 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D).

Step 2: Conclusion
NAA and 2,4-D are purely synthetic auxins.

answer.text: NAA and 2, 4-D
IAA and IBA
IAA and NAA
IBA and 2, 4-D

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q32 - Apical dominance and decapitation application

questiontext.text: In most higher plants, the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of lateral (axillary) buds. What is this phenomenon called, and which practical procedure overcomes it in tea plantations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying apical dominance
The inhibition of lateral bud outgrowth by the growing apical bud is termed apical dominance, mediated predominantly by apical auxin synthesis.

Step 2: Practical management
Removal of shoot tips (decapitation) removes the source of auxin, which allows lateral buds to grow into bushy lateral branches. This is widely used in tea plantations and hedge-making.

Step 3: Conclusion
The phenomenon is apical dominance, overcome by shoot tip decapitation.

answer.text: Apical dominance; decapitation (removal of shoot tips)
Bolting; spraying gibberellic acid
Parthenocarpy; applying high concentrations of abscisic acid
Plasticity; submerged pruning of leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q33 - Selective weedicide action of synthetic auxin 2 4 D

questiontext.text: The synthetic auxin 2, 4-D (2, 4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) is widely used by gardeners to prepare weed-free lawns because it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the herbicidal action of 2, 4-D
2, 4-D is a selective systemic herbicide.

Step 2: Differential susceptibility
It is widely used to kill broad-leaved dicotyledonous weeds while having no adverse effect on mature monocotyledonous plants (such as grasses in a lawn).

Step 3: Conclusion
2, 4-D selectively kills broad-leaved dicotyledonous weeds without affecting mature monocots.

answer.text: Kills broad-leaved dicotyledonous weeds without affecting mature monocotyledonous plants
Destroys all monocotyledonous grass species while stimulating dicot weeds
Inhibits seed germination indiscriminately in all plant species
Causes instant stomatal closure leading to total dehydration of lawn turf

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q34 - Physiological effects attributed to auxins

questiontext.text: Which of the following physiological effects is correctly attributed to auxins in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reviewing physiological effects of auxins
Auxins:
- Initiate rooting in stem cuttings.
- Promote flowering in pineapples.
- Prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages, but promote abscission of older, mature leaves and fruits.
- Induce parthenocarpy in tomatoes.
- Control xylem differentiation and cell division.

Step 2: Conclusion
Auxins prevent premature fruit and leaf drop at early stages while promoting the abscission of older mature leaves and fruits.

answer.text: Preventing fruit and leaf drop at early stages while promoting abscission of older organs
Accelerating the malting process in the brewing industry
Inducing respiratory climacteric during fruit ripening
Promoting bolting in beet and cabbage prior to flowering

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q35 - Effect of gibberellin spray on sugarcane yield

questiontext.text: Sugarcane stores carbohydrates as sugar in its stems. Spraying a sugarcane crop with gibberellins increases the yield by as much as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the specific effect on sugarcane
Gibberellins stimulate internodal elongation along the plant axis.

Step 2: Quantitative yield increase
NCERT explicitly states that spraying sugarcane crops with gibberellins increases the length of the stem, thereby increasing the yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.

Step 3: Conclusion
The yield increases by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.

answer.text: 20 tonnes per acre
5 tonnes per acre
50 tonnes per acre
10 tonnes per acre

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q36 - Bolting induced by gibberellins

questiontext.text: What is the term used to describe internode elongation just prior to flowering in rosette plants like beet and cabbages, and which hormone promotes it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Defining the phenomenon
In rosette plants like beet, cabbage, and many others, internodes remain compressed during vegetative growth. Just prior to flowering, these internodes rapidly elongate.

Step 2: Phytohormone responsible
This sudden elongation of internodes prior to flowering is termed 'bolting', and it is promoted by gibberellins (GAs).

Step 3: Conclusion
The phenomenon is bolting, induced by gibberellins.

answer.text: Bolting; promoted by gibberellins
Apical dominance; promoted by auxins
Senescence; promoted by abscisic acid
Parthenocarpy; promoted by cytokinins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q37 - Industrial applications of gibberellic acid GA3

questiontext.text: Which of the following applications in the food and beverage industry relies on gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluating functions of GA3
\(\text{GA}_3\) produces diverse commercial effects:
- Used to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry.
- Increases length of grape stalks.
- Causes fruits like apple to elongate and improve their shape.
- Delays senescence so fruits remain on trees longer to extend market period.

Step 2: Conclusion
\(\text{GA}_3\) is specifically utilized to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry.

answer.text: Speeding up the malting process in the brewing industry
Inducing uniform fruit-drop to thin out apple orchards
Accelerating ethylene production in sealed banana ripening chambers
Inhibiting \(\alpha\)-amylase synthesis in germinating barley seeds

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q38 - Natural occurrence and isolation of cytokinins

questiontext.text: Regarding cytokinins, which of the following statements is correct regarding kinetin and zeatin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Origin of kinetin
Kinetin was discovered from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and does not occur naturally in plants.

Step 2: Origin of zeatin
Search for natural compounds with cytokinin-like activity led to the isolation of zeatin from corn-kernels and coconut milk.

Step 3: Conclusion
Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants, whereas zeatin is a naturally occurring cytokinin isolated from corn-kernels and coconut milk.

answer.text: Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants, whereas zeatin was isolated from corn-kernels and coconut milk
Both kinetin and zeatin were directly crystallized from human urine
Zeatin is a synthetic auxin, while kinetin is a naturally occurring carotenoid derivative
Kinetin was isolated from oat coleoptile tips and zeatin from rice seedlings

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q39 - Sites of synthesis and physiological roles of cytokinins

questiontext.text: Natural cytokinins are synthesized predominantly in regions where rapid cell division occurs. Which of the following is a primary physiological role of cytokinins?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying synthesis sites
Natural cytokinins are synthesized in regions of active cell division: root apices, developing shoot buds, and young fruits.

Step 2: Identifying physiological actions
Cytokinins:
- Promote production of new leaves and chloroplasts in leaves.
- Promote lateral shoot growth and adventitious shoot formation.
- Help overcome apical dominance.
- Promote nutrient mobilization which helps in delaying leaf senescence.

Step 3: Conclusion
Cytokinins help overcome apical dominance and promote nutrient mobilization that delays leaf senescence.

answer.text: Overcoming apical dominance and promoting nutrient mobilization to delay leaf senescence
Maintaining seed dormancy and inducing immediate stomatal closure
Thinning of flowers and fruits in cotton, cherry, and walnut
Inducing horizontal triple response growth in seedlings

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q40 - Triple response and seedling growth influenced by ethylene

questiontext.text: Which group of morphological responses in dicot seedlings is typically induced by the gaseous plant hormone ethylene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying ethylene responses in seedlings
NCERT states: "Influences of ethylene on plants include horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings."

Step 2: Conclusion
Horizontal growth of seedlings, axis swelling, and apical hook formation represent the classic ethylene response in dicot seedlings.

answer.text: Horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis, and apical hook formation
Rapid vertical axis elongation, thinning of the stem, and inhibition of rooting
Apical bud dormancy, degradation of chloroplasts, and stomatal opening
Extreme elongation of internodes, absence of hooks, and prevention of abscission

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q41 - Respiratory climacteric in fruit ripening

questiontext.text: During the ripening of fleshy fruits, ethylene causes a sharp enhancement in the rate of respiration. What is this phenomenon termed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the metabolic effect of ethylene during ripening
Ethylene is highly effective in promoting fruit ripening. Along with softening and color transformation, it dramatically increases the respiration rate of the tissue.

Step 2: Terminology
This sharp rise in the rate of cellular respiration during ripening is termed "respiratory climactic" (or respiratory climacteric).

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct term is respiratory climactic.

answer.text: Respiratory climactic
Photorespiration burst
Pasteur effect
Efficiency index surge

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q42 - Agricultural applications of ethephon

questiontext.text: Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene in agricultural practice. Which of the following statements about ethephon is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Properties of ethephon
Ethephon in an aqueous solution is readily absorbed and transported within the plant and releases ethylene gas slowly.

Step 2: Agricultural applications
- Hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples.
- Accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut).
- Promotes female flowers in cucumbers, thereby increasing yield.

Step 3: Conclusion
Ethephon accelerates abscission/thinning in cotton, cherry, and walnut, and promotes female flowers in cucumbers.

answer.text: It releases ethylene slowly, thins walnut and cherry fruits, and increases female flowers in cucumbers
It prevents fruit abscission indefinitely and inhibits female flower production in cucurbits
It is an insoluble solid powder that cannot be transported through plant vascular tissues
It exclusively stimulates shoot apical dominance in conifers

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q43 - Role of ethylene in deep water rice plants

questiontext.text: How does ethylene facilitate the survival of deep water rice plants during flooding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the specific adaptation in deep water rice
Submerged organs of deep water rice experience rapid gas accumulation.

Step 2: Mechanism of action
Ethylene promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation in deep water rice plants. This allows the leaves and upper parts of the shoot to remain above water level, ensuring continuous gaseous exchange and photosynthesis.

Step 3: Conclusion
Ethylene promotes rapid elongation of internodes and petioles to keep foliage above the water surface.

answer.text: Promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation so upper foliage remains above water
Closes stomata completely and halts all respiratory processes
Induces heavy secondary wall deposition in aerenchyma to prevent water entry
Causes immediate abscission of all underwater leaves to prevent decay

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q44 - Physiological functions of abscisic acid ABA

questiontext.text: Abscisic acid (ABA) is widely recognized as a stress hormone because it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying stress responses
Under water deficit and environmental stress, ABA levels rise sharply.

Step 2: Primary mechanisms
ABA stimulates the rapid closure of stomata to minimize transpirational water loss and increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of stresses. Additionally, it induces seed dormancy, helping seeds survive desiccation and adverse environments.

Step 3: Conclusion
ABA stimulates stomatal closure and enhances plant tolerance to multiple stresses.

answer.text: Stimulates the closure of stomata and increases plant tolerance to various environmental stresses
Triggers immediate flowering in pineapples during prolonged periods of drought
Increases \(\alpha\)-amylase production in barley seeds to speed up starch breakdown
Reverses xylem differentiation to enhance water conduction under drought

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q45 - Antagonistic relationship between ABA and GA

questiontext.text: In most physiological situations, particularly regarding seed dormancy and germination, abscisic acid (ABA) acts as an antagonist to which plant growth regulator?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying hormone interactions
Hormonal control of development involves synergistic and antagonistic pairs.

Step 2: Evaluating ABA interactions
Gibberellins (GAs) break dormancy, stimulate hydrolytic enzyme synthesis, and promote seed germination. In contrast, ABA inhibits germination and establishes/maintains seed dormancy. Thus, ABA acts as an antagonist to gibberellins.

Step 3: Conclusion
ABA acts as an antagonist to gibberellins (GAs).

answer.text: Gibberellins (GAs)
Auxins exclusively
Ethylene
Kinetin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q46 - Root growth and root hair formation promoted by ethylene

questiontext.text: A plant physiologist intends to increase the absorption surface area of seedling root systems. Which plant growth regulator promotes root growth and root hair formation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the specific physiological role
Increasing the absorption surface area of roots requires root hair differentiation and lateral root proliferation.

Step 2: NCERT verification
NCERT explicitly states under Section 13.4.3.4: "Ethylene also promotes root growth and root hair formation, thus helping the plants to increase their absorption surface."

Step 3: Conclusion
Ethylene is responsible for promoting root hair formation and root growth to maximize absorption surface.

answer.text: Ethylene
Abscisic acid
Gibberellic acid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q47 - Speeding seed production in juvenile conifers

questiontext.text: Spraying juvenile conifers with which plant growth regulator hastens their maturity period, thereby leading to early seed production?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the specific application
Conifers generally possess a prolonged juvenile phase before entering the reproductive phase.

Step 2: Textbook evidence
NCERT explicitly states: "Spraying juvenile conifers with GAs hastens the maturity period, thus leading to early seed production."

Step 3: Conclusion
Gibberellins (GAs) hasten maturity and early seed production in juvenile conifers.

answer.text: Gibberellins (GAs)
Abscisic acid (ABA)
Cytokinins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q48 - Hormonal induction of flowering in pineapples

questiontext.text: Which two plant growth regulators are explicitly cited in the text as being capable of promoting or initiating flowering and synchronizing fruit-set in pineapples?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying mentions of flowering in pineapple
1. Under Section 13.4.3.1 (Auxins): "Auxins promote flowering e.g. in pineapples."
2. Under Section 13.4.3.4 (Ethylene): "Ethylene is used to initiate flowering and for synchronising fruit-set in pineapples."

Step 2: Conclusion
Both auxins and ethylene promote or initiate flowering in pineapples.

answer.text: Auxins and Ethylene
Gibberellins and Abscisic acid
Cytokinins and Abscisic acid
Gibberellins and Cytokinins
